KEY MESSAGE 1...
Upper air analysis this early morning depicts the base of a 
positively-tilted, shortwave trough pivoting eastward over Lake 
Erie, with convergent flow on the backside of this departing trough 
yielding a clear sky across the lowlands and most of the higher 
terrain. The exception is the northeastern mountains of WV, where 
orographically-induced stratus persists; however, this stratus deck 
should dissipate by sunrise as drier air aloft continues advecting 
into the region. Satellite imagery also depicts a corridor of river 
valley fog to the east of the I-79 corridor, and it is possible that 
additional riverine systems develop steam fog through the predawn 
hours as surface temperatures continue to rapidly cool and as the 
boundary-layer decouples. Patchy fog previously introduced by the 
prior shift has been maintained with this prognostication, with any 
fog dissipating by the late-morning hours.

At the surface, the primary synoptic cold front stemming from a 
cyclone rotating into Newfoundland has moved into the Atlantic 
Ocean, with a weaker, secondary cold front sagging southward towards 
the Niagara Frontier. Farther west, the centroid of a polar surface 
high, analyzed at 1036 mb (and rising), was rotating into the Upper 
Midwest. The secondary cold front will undergo frontolysis and 
transition into a diffuse surface trough as continues to migrate 
southward towards the region today, with surface winds veering 
northeastward as the aforementioned polar anticyclone continues to 
rotate towards the CWA. The 24/00Z RAOBs from WFOs ILN and PBZ 
observed a deep subsidence layer/warm nose, owing to the arrival of 
a low-amplitude, shortwave ridge. Vertical mixing heights this 
afternoon will be shunted by the presence of this strong inversion 
and keep high temperatures on the chilly side today. 

Temperatures will crater once again tonight, with Wednesday morning 
lows falling into the middle 20s across the majority of the lowlands 
and into portions of the higher terrain. Lows in the upper teens are 
now explicitly forecast across the northeastern mountains of WV 
tonight. As the strengthening polar surface high continues rotating 
eastward into the northern Appalachian Mountains tonight, winds will 
veer towards the east accordingly. The tightened pressure gradient 
will garner easterly gusts in the 20-30 mph range across the higher 
terrain tonight, yielding wind chill values in the lower teens for 
those locales. Easterly winds will persist Wednesday, resulting in 
warmer temperatures, albeit still chilly in the mountains, with 
highs peaking in the middle 50s across the lowlands. Increasing 
cloud cover is expected Wednesday ahead of a potent storm system 
beginning to materialize to the south of the CWA.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Precipitation chances are set to increase Wednesday night into 
Thanksgiving morning, as an intensifying storm system tracks 
poleward along the Eastern Seaboard. In the mid/upper-levels, a 
split-flow pattern will persist across the Lower 48, characterized 
by a pair of shortwave troughs traversing the central U.S. that will
phase into a large-scale trough over the Deep South come Wednesday 
night. The northern-stream trough, previously emanating from a 
large, baroclinic system offshore the Pacific Northwest, will 
feature a well-defined vorticity lobe as it digs southeastward over 
the Missouri River Valley and phases with the open, southern-stream 
trough ejecting over the northern Gulf Coast. This is forecast to 
result in the genesis of closed, negatively-tilted trough digging 
into the southeastern U.S. heading into Thanksgiving. The vortex 
will be substantially misaligned as the negatively-tilted trough 
begins to evolve, with the attendant surface low deepening to the 
south of the Outer Banks. As this evolution occurs, an enlarged, 
baroclinic leaf will develop in congruence with a particularly 
intense belt of divergent outflow aloft as flow throughout the 
base of the phasing trough(s) remains subgeostrophic. 

A rapid increase in DPVA and the related moistening of the theta 
surfaces across the entire Eastern Seaboard will advect a plume of 
high PWAT content into the region, with PWATs climbing above 1.00" 
across the CWA as the rain shield arrives Wednesday night. The 
strong WAA regime associated with this system despite the presence 
of a northeasterly fetch will warrant much warmer low temperatures 
Thanksgiving morning, with lows in the upper 30s and lower 40s for 
most of the CWA. Moderate to localized pockets of heavy rainfall are 
in store across the region Thanksgiving morning, with a cold rain 
forecast in the mountains where surface temperatures may reach 32 
degrees. Strong/warm, low-level theta-e advection from the easterly
